title: Cosmic Cotton Candy: Astronomers Find Two Planets Lighter Than Fairy Floss
summary: Imagine a world the size of Jupiter but so insubstantial it could float on water—if you had an ocean large enough. Astronomers have identified two such planets, TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, orbiting a star 1,110 light-years away in the constellation Volans. Their densities are astonishing: 0.038 and 0.047 grams per cubic centimeter, respectively. That's less than cotton candy (about 0.05 g/cm³) and roughly 30 times less dense than Jupiter. These "super-puff" planets are among the fluffiest ever found. The discovery, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, was led by an international team including the University of Oxford. The planets are locked in a 5:3 mean-motion resonance: for every five orbits of the inner world, the outer completes three. This gravitational interplay causes slight timing variations in their transits, allowing scientists to calculate their masses—and hence their incredibly low densities. "Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system," said the lead author. "Their extremely low densities make them fascinating targets for understanding how planetary systems form and evolve." The planets were first flagged by volunteers in the Planet Hunters TESS citizen-science project, which scours data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. Follow-up observations included eight years of data, notably from the ASTEP telescope in Antarctica, where months of uninterrupted winter darkness allowed continuous monitoring of the planets' unusually long transits—each lasting over 11 hours, the longest ever fully observed from the ground. Scientists believe these worlds possess vast atmospheres of hydrogen and helium, possibly accumulated in the cold outer regions of their protoplanetary disc before migrating inward. Future observations aim to test competing theories of how such ethereal giants come to be. For now, they remain a delightful cosmic oddity—proof that the universe still has plenty of surprises.
why_it_matters: These fluffy planets force scientists to rethink how worlds are assembled, and understanding their fragile atmospheres can teach us about the extremes of planetary evolution—which in turn helps us see our own solar system’s history in a new light. It’s a perfect example of how citizen science and global collaboration can make surprising discoveries.

background_read: NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) scans nearly the whole sky to catch the faint dimming of stars when planets cross in front; the Planet Hunters TESS citizen-science project lets volunteers from around the world examine those light curves online.

The ASTEP telescope (Antarctic Search for Transiting ExoPlanets) at Concordia Station in Antarctica benefits from months of continuous winter darkness, enabling it to watch planet transits that last many hours without a break from daylight.

The University of Oxford (a prestigious university in the United Kingdom, founded in the 11th century) was part of the international team that published the findings in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, a major astronomy journal.

Mean-motion resonances occur when two planets’ orbital periods are related by a ratio of small integers; this creates subtle gravitational kicks that slightly alter transit timings, allowing scientists to weigh the planets.

Super-puffs like TOI-791 b and c challenge standard theories of planet formation because their extremely low densities mean they must be mostly atmosphere; understanding them may shed light on how gas giants like Jupiter evolved.

perspectives.description: The discovery provides a natural laboratory to test planet formation theories. Super-puffs cannot be explained by standard models, so they push researchers to refine ideas about how gas accumulates and how close-in planets survive, potentially leading to breakthroughs in exoplanet science.

Some theorists worry that such extremely low-density planets might not be stable over long timescales; the intense radiation from their star could rapidly strip away the lightweight atmospheres, meaning we caught them in a brief, unlikely stage. This raises doubts about whether they represent a common class of planets or a temporary anomaly.

The 5:3 resonance suggests the two planets formed together and experienced a shared migration history, making the system a clean case study for orbital dynamics and disc-planet interactions. By comparing their current state with simulations, researchers can measure how much mass has been lost over time.

The James Webb Space Telescope and upcoming ground-based instruments could probe the atmospheres of these super-puffs for chemical signatures, revealing their temperature structure and wind speeds. Such data may help distinguish between the competing theories—whether the planets formed in situ or migrated—and could identify other systems with similar fluffiness.
